frames.narration: The table holds 500,000 users in the order they signed up. The query is: find the user with this email.
Without an index the database has only one option: read every row and compare its email. This is a full table scan.
Row after row, until it reaches the match. Twice the rows means twice the work, and every user logging in pays this cost.
Now create an index on email: a sorted list of emails, each with a pointer to its row. The database maintains it automatically.
The same query now searches the index. Because it is sorted, each step discards half of what is left.
The index returns a pointer, and the database jumps straight to that one row.
19 steps instead of 500,000. Double the table and it is about one step more. That is the point of an index.
The price: every insert or update must also update the index, so writes get slower and the index uses extra space. Add indexes for the queries you really run.
